item.title: Evolution and breakdown of chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium
item.description: arXiv:2610.13084v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chiral anomaly in topological materials manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, yet the tunability and evolution of this effect remain elusive. Here we show that doped tellurium serves as a versatile platform to realize a giant negative longitudinal magnetoresistance that is highly tunable via the Fermi level and magnetic field. By moving the Fermi level towards the Weyl point, we observe a pronounced enhancement of negative magnetoresistance, which arises from chiral anomaly and robustly persists up to ambient temperature. Beyond the quantum limit, the system exhibits positive linear magnetoconductance, serving as a compelling transport signature of the chiral anomaly in the lowest Landau level. Notably, in the extreme quantum limit at cryogenic temperatures, the magnetoresistance undergoes a dramatic reversal from negative to positive. This reversal points to a potential field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state driven by enhanced electron-electron interactions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the unconventional chiral transport and emergent correlated quantum states under extreme magnetic fields.

item.title: Latin squares as a model of perfect mixing of high-entropy alloys
item.description: arXiv:2610.13519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The structure of high-entropy alloys, which include 5 or more components in equimolar proportions, is proposed to be described in the mathematical language of Latin squares. This model is fundamentally discrete and allows for a quantitative description of ideal mixing, in which any given alloy element is guaranteed not to have an identical element as its nearest neighbor. For the two-dimensional case, the model possesses four axes of translational symmetry, which makes it possible to tile the plane with a single Latin square and, based on the properties of this square, describe the properties of macroscopic material samples. The model makes it possible to make quantitative estimates of the suitability of a particular atomic structure (configuration) for implementation in a perfectly mixed high-entropy alloy with maximum mixing entropy. A condition has been obtained for acceptable fluctuations in the concentration of components at which the thermodynamic stability of the alloy is maintained. The possibility of identifying superstructures in high-entropy alloys based on group theory, as applied to the description and construction of Latin squares, is discussed. Based on the proposed model, the probability of forming a multicomponent alloy with ideal mixing is estimated. For a five-component alloy, this probability is no more than 2.6*10^{-10}.
item.dc:creator: P. S. Grinchuk

item.title: UV Fluorescence Sensing of Medical-Chemical-and- Biological Analytes by an AlGaN/Si-on-Sapphire Optoelectronic Chip
item.description: arXiv:2610.13525v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes and analyzes a compact fluorescence-photometer lab-on-a-chip that is simpler than a fluorescence spectrometer, and that does not require spectrum reconstruction by a computer. An on-chip AlGaN VCSEL lasing at 280 nm, or at 310 nm, pumps an on-chip sample in the form of liquid or solid or tissue, thereby exciting signature fluorescence in the 300 to 540 nm wavelength range. This emission signal is detected and read out by an on-chip UV-enhanced Silicon photodiode. The 2 cm x 5 cm chip consists of C-plane (0001) Sapphire, and no lenses, prisms, or mirrors are utilized in the photometer. The chip is opto-electronic and features co-packaged electronics using tiny electronic chiplets that are bonded to the sapphire. These consist of an LD driver and transimpedance amplifier for the UV photonics, together with ASICs, ADC, microcontroller, micro-battery and RF-wireless or Ethernet chiplets. The mission of this self-contained cost-effective chip is sensing targeted medical-chemical-biological (MCB) agents in a local or network setting. Eight significant MCB applications are detailed here.
item.dc:creator: Richard Soref

item.title: Thin-film nanostructuring of NbTi superconducting resonators for enhanced temperature sensitivity in cryogenic thermometry
item.description: arXiv:2605.01915v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rising complexity of cutting-edge cryogenic systems is currently imposing challenging technical constraints to the monitoring of ultra-cold temperatures through standard commercially available sensors. Among different technologies, superconducting microwave resonators have been recently investigated as ideal candidates for performing on-chip cryogenic thermometry, in reason of their intrinsically low power dissipation, large temperature sensitivities and excellent sub-$\mu$K resolution below 10 K. Through this study, we aim at demonstrating the possibility to enhance the temperature performance of superconducting microwave resonators by means of surface nanostructuring. Different arrays of nanotrenches are strategically patterned on the inductive line of a 1.3 GHz planar resonator, by partially etching a Nb$_{50}$Ti$_{50}$ thin-film, in order to tune the critical transition of the material and, therefore, increase the curvature of the $f_{res}(T)$ response. Although the presence of such thinned superconducting regions introduces larger microwave losses, a 1.5 K decrease of $T_\text{C}$ is recorded, which directly translates into an enhancement of the temperature sensitivity by a factor 10, with respect to a non-nanostructured sensor. A maximum value of $df_{res}/dT = 62 \ \text{MHz/K}$, at 4.2 K, is achieved for the device showing the largest nanotrench width of about 350 nm. These results demonstrate that such a surface nanostructuring approach can be exploited as an effective design strategy to tune the $f_{res}(T)$ response of superconducting microwave resonators. Although this technique is found to introduce additional RF losses into the superconducting device, thereby limiting the achievable temperature resolution to the few-$\mu\text{K/Hz}^{1/2}$ range, we believe that similar approaches could be further investigated for the development of future cryogenic sensors.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'e Chatel, Roberto Russo, Seyed Alireza Hashemi, Pol Torres-Vila, J\"urgen Brugger, Giovanni Boero, Hern\'an Furci

item.title: Towards Accurate MHz Core Loss Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.07596v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Miniaturized magnetic components play an important role in achieving high efficiency and high power density in power converters. Accurate core loss data are essential when optimizing magnetic components, but making accurate core loss measurements remains challenging, especially at MHz frequencies. As a result, many research groups have developed their own testers in pursuit of improved accuracy, and the amount of published core loss data has increased. However, large variations in these data shed light on fundamental barriers to accurate MHz core loss measurement. This paper identifies these barriers and presents methods for overcoming them.
item.dc:creator: Nick J. Kirkby, Mike K. Ranjram
